articles.summary:
DoubleZero has launched a dedicated fiber-optic market data feed for Hyperliquid, providing professional trading firms with faster, more consistent access to the decentralized exchange’s full order book.

### Key Points
- The new service provides a continuous, ordered stream of market data for perpetual futures and assets like gold, oil, and silver.
- Development partners for the feed include validator operators and ecosystem firms such as Hyperion DeFi, MAVAN, and Kinetiq.
- The feed replaces the need for firms to manually assemble data from public APIs or operate their own individual Hyperliquid nodes.
- DoubleZero’s Edge service now supports three venues, having previously integrated data feeds for the Solana blockchain and the prediction market Kalshi.
- The infrastructure is designed specifically for market makers and quantitative trading firms requiring high-speed, reliable order book updates.

### Why it Matters
This development signals a shift as onchain markets adopt the specialized data distribution models long utilized by traditional electronic exchanges like the CME or Nasdaq. While the service does not enable faster trade execution, it standardizes professional-grade data access to support the growing institutional presence within decentralized finance.

articles.title: Apple has three products launching soon that we’ve waited a long time for
articles.author: Ryan Christoffel
articles.content:
Apple had a big September, but it’s set to keep momentum going in October with several rumored product unveilings soon that we’ve waited a long time for.
#1: MacBook Pro / Ultra redesign with touchscreen
The Mac is a long-time touchscreen holdout, but that’s finally set to change with a new MacBook Pro (or MacBook Ultra) product expected to launch in October.
Apple’s next-gen MacBook Pro will introduce a brand new industrial design—the first such overhaul in five years. And in addition to touch support, it will boast an OLED display, Dynamic Island, and possibly a C2 cellular modem option.
It’s been a long time since the MacBook Pro got a new look. But far longer since touchscreens became the norm, and Apple decided to forego them on the Mac. I’m excited to see how touch might enhance the experience of the Mac moving forward.
#2: New Apple TV 4K
There’s never been a longer wait for new Apple TV hardware than the current drought of updates. Apple’s latest model, the third-gen Apple TV 4K, was introduced in 2022.
Rumors indicate we’ll finally get a new Apple TV 4K in October, headlined by a powerful A19 or A19 Pro chip and Siri AI support.
This summer Apple raised prices on most of its products, including the Apple TV. That means the four-year-old Apple TV 4K now costs $199—far more than the $129 price it launched at. Here’s hoping the new Apple TV doesn’t go any higher.
#3: ‘HomePad’
Rumors of a HomePod with a display have been around for nearly as long as the HomePod’s existence. But they ramped up in 2024 when Mark Gurman offered an in-depth report on what’s commonly called the ‘HomePad.’
Top comment by Billy Coker
Personally, I don't want to see another article about Apple TV until the thing comes out. It's always "Coming soon", "Coming soon", and it never shows
HomePad is a smart display with built-in speaker that will reportedly spearhead Apple’s renewed push into home products. It will have a new OS that resembles parts of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS, including a StandBy-like mode.
Siri AI is expected to be central to the product, which will also feature a camera, customizable widgets, and built-in Apple apps like Photos, Notes, Music, Calendar, and more.
Which new Apple products in October and beyond are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.
articles.summary:
Apple is reportedly preparing to launch several new hardware products in October, including a redesigned MacBook Pro, an updated Apple TV 4K, and a smart display device.

### Key Points
- The upcoming MacBook Pro will feature a significant industrial redesign, including a touchscreen, an OLED display, and a potential C2 cellular modem.
- A new Apple TV 4K is expected to debut with an A19 or A19 Pro chip and integrated Siri AI capabilities.
- The rumored "HomePad" smart display will combine speaker functionality with a camera and a new operating system featuring customizable widgets.
- The HomePad OS will incorporate elements from iOS, tvOS, and watchOS to support native applications like Photos, Notes, and Music.

### Why it Matters
These product updates represent a strategic expansion of Apple’s ecosystem into the smart home market and a major shift in its long-standing laptop design philosophy. By integrating advanced AI and touchscreen technology, the company aims to maintain its competitive edge against rivals in both the personal computing and home automation sectors.

articles.title: Oh no, here come the AI Tamagotchis
articles.author: Daniel Bader
articles.content:
Good morning. Today I’m watching yet another Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave review (watch this for context), getting started on my Booker Prize shortlist read-through, and reading as much as I can about Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” now that it’s the longest-running #1 hit of all time.
As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.
Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.
⭐️ Starred
Meta may no longer be a metaverse company, but it’s trying its damndest to be a hardware company. At last night’s Meta Connect event, the company unveiled a bunch of new AI wearables, including the third-generation Ray-Ban Meta camera glasses, the camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, a wider rollout of its Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, and a next-gen VR product called, appropriately, Meta VR Glasses, coming in the spring of 2027.
All of these are interesting in their own way, particularly the VR Glasses, which are basically Galaxy XR/Vision Pro competitors in a much smaller form factor and considerably lower cost ($1,299). Meta’s found considerable traction with its bevy of wearables despite growing pushback from privacy advocates and regular people who don’t want to be filmed with “perv glasses.” The audio-only product, which boasts Dolby Atmos support, is a direct response to that, but the company is still iterating on the baseline camera hardware while promising software updates will prevent misuse.
But the really interesting announcement came in the form of a Tamagotchi-like doohickey called the Muse Charm that runs Meta’s popular new Muse AI agent, which has seen massive growth as an app on Android, iOS, and Mac. The hardware has a 2-inch OLED touch display, a camera and microphones, a 5G modem, and runs a proprietary OS that Meta says will connect to retailers like Walmart and Best Buy.
AI agents are no longer novel — I’ve been testing them all summer in the form of apps like Poke, Tolan, Instinct, Town, and others — but Muse has taken off because it’s free, fast, and genuinely useful. Meta is also building it into everything it owns, from Instagram to WhatsApp, and is soon adding the ability to chat with an agent through video.
At the beginning of 2024, we had a few months of hand-wringing over AI gadgets like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin, but they failed because the models were not even close to being ready for the tasks promised in the marketing. Now, AI agents are more than capable of chasing down a refund, booking a concert, or buying an anniversary gift, and Meta’s preemptive jump into the space will only heighten expectations for OpenAI’s rumored hardware product that’s expected to debut in 2027.
I regret to inform you, though: I think the Museagotchi looks pretty damn cute.
✉️ Inbox
- Adobe Premiere for Android launches for free with layered video editing, YouTube templates. I feel like we’ve been waiting years for Premiere on Android, and it’s finally here. And free, which is pretty great.
- Samsung has delayed its Android 17 update. By a week. We’ll be fine.
- Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Qualcomm is going to five blades this year with its new dual flagship chip strategy. The Elite Gen 6 is the standard one, with the Extreme boasting “advanced agentic AI” capabilities.
- Oppo Find X10 series goes official with triple 200MP cameras, 8,000 mAh battery. I can’t even with this phone. Monster specs and a ridiculous camera array, sure. But a battery that size? I need it right now.
- Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Oh, I guess 8,000 mAh wasn’t big enough.
- Android Auto rolls out game support, no longer in beta. I know that this exists just to compete with Tesla, but I genuinely don’t know why this is legal.
- Motorola Signature 27 is a proper flagship with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. This phone will probably cost $2,000 but holy smokes does it look worth it.
- Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Sol & Luna both launch today with lower costs. I’ve been testing both of these models and if this is what “pacing the frontier” looks like, we’re all doomed (in a good way).
- Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra leak shows another side, confirming minimal changes. A $1000+ Android tablet? In this economy?
- Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak. This is genuinely the funniest thing I’ve heard all week. Only Google could make this happen.
- YouTube announces Custom Feeds, GIF comments, and ‘Your podcast lineup’. YouTube’s making some interesting announcements in the face of increasing competition from Netflix in the “clips” space.
- Google Beam 3D meeting booths coming to co-working spaces. Remember the sci-fi-esque video conferencing booths that Google debuted a few years ago under the Starline name? Well, they’re still a kajillion dollars, but they seem popular enough to be expanding to co-working spaces in Atlanta, Chicago, New York City, and Palo Alto.
- Google Maps update shows traffic lights and stop signs at your next turn on Android Auto, more
- Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too
➡️ FWD:
I’m going to do a bit of shameless self-promotion today and share a few cool things that the 9to5 video team has been working on.
Our Googlebook hands-on video is close to 500k views, and for good reason: Jordan absolutely crushes it with his deep dive into the highs, lows, and oddities of Google’s latest hardware launch.
Damien does a spectacular job detailing life with Google’s $899 Pixel 11, noting that “there is a good phone underneath the price hikes,” but that $100 bump really overshadows the battery and camera improvements.
Finally, I was back on The Sideload with my buddy, Will Sattelberg, where we had the privilege of talking to Kevin Michaluk and Jeff Gadway of Clicks, which is about to release its long-awaited Communicator smartphone this December. It was a really fun conversation that gets a bit philosophical about why we use technology and what it really means to disconnect in today’s world.
And if you missed my Cc: questions with Kevin from Tuesday’s Inbox edition, you can catch up with them here.
🗑️ Trash
Disney+ is raising its prices for the fourth time in four years. The popular Disney+ Premium plan with no ads now runs $21.49, a 13% bump over yesterday’s price.
Just this year, Netflix, Peacock, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, and Paramount Plus got more expensive, and it seems that every streamer is making their ad-free tier as unenticing as possible to lure people back to ads.
I’m pretty close to canceling Netflix — my kids watch a fair amount of its fare — but I happily canceled Disney+ the last time prices went up, and I wouldn’t be surprised if a few thousand subscribers did the same just now.
With FAST services like Pluto TV, Tubi, The Roku Channel, Freevee, and many more offering a decent assortment of free content in exchange for a network television-level of ad density, it really does seem like all roads do eventually lead to cable.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.
Thanks for reading, and have a great day. Talk to you on Tuesday.
-Daniel

articles.title: The best upgrade I made to my smart TV was turning these “smart” features off
articles.author: Kanika Gogia
articles.content:
When I bought my shiny smart TV, I was excited to use all the smart features it offers. Well, why not? I thought these clever features would make a smart TV smarter.
After using my TV for a while, I realized I didn’t even use or need every "smart" feature. My TV was constantly suggesting things I didn’t want to watch and promoted unwanted content on the home screen. I took the charge and started turning them off one by one.
The result? My home screen felt less cluttered, and I stopped feeling as if I was being watched in my living room. Also, it made my TV a lot better to use.
Home screen ads and Autoplay
I don’t want my TV selling me things
The first thing that annoyed me was how my home screen was filled with ads and promotional offers. Rather than a neat app launcher, my home screen looked like a marketplace: sponsored titles, banner ads, and whatnot. I crave a clean and simple home screen, so I decided to turn off ads and promotional content.
On my LG OLED TV, I opened All Settings -> General -> System -> Additional Settings -> Home Settings and disabled the Home Promotion option. The exact steps depend on the TV model that you own. On Roku or Samsung TVs, you can find a similar option (advertising) in Privacy settings.
Beyond this, I also turned off the Autoplay option. I find it super annoying when I’m browsing the home screen to decide what to watch, and my TV starts autoplaying a blaring trailer I’m not interested in. Once I disabled Autoplay, my home screen felt faster, and there’s less clutter (and noise, too).
Automatic content recognition
I don’t want another layer of tracking, please
Automatic content recognition (ACR) is one of those features that keeps running in the background and consumes unnecessary processing power, and most of us don’t even realize it.
The basic idea is pretty simple. Your TV keeps an eye on what you’re watching to understand your usage habits and interests. It then uses this information for viewing-related recommendations or audience insights. It depends on the manufacturer and the permissions you've agreed to. The manufacturer can also share this information with third-party advertisers and make some money. Frankly speaking, ACR doesn’t offer much for viewers. So, turning it off won’t break anything.
It’s worth knowing that the exact name varies between manufacturers. So, you might not see an option literally called "ACR." You might see something like Live Plus (LG TVs), Viewing Information, Interactive TV, or similar. If you’re setting up a smart TV, it's a great idea to turn off this feature right away.
Energy-saving features
This might sound strange
I know, energy-saving is a good thing. But some energy-saving settings can affect the picture quality of your TV. On most smart TVs, energy-saving mode is enabled by default. This reduces the panel brightness and contrast for HDR content, resulting in a dim and less vibrant picture quality. This isn’t ideal if you’re watching high-quality content or have placed your TV in a bright room.
Picture quality and contrast are some of the big reasons why I bought a high-end OLED TV. I don’t want my TV to constantly change brightness because of some power-saving setting. I decided to disable energy-saving mode on my TV. As soon as I did it, the HDR content appeared richer with deeper blacks and punchier highlights. Also, my TV no longer dims unpredictably during dark scenes.
Motion smoothing
Smoother isn’t always better
Another setting I changed was Motion smoothing, and it made a huge difference in the way my TV looks. Depending on the TV brand you own, this setting might be called TruMotion, MotionFlow, Auto Motion Plus, or Action Smoothing. Most movies are shot at 24 fps, while modern TVs refresh at 60 or 120 Hz.
Basically, motion smoothing generates artificial in-between frames to make everything look fluid. It reduces blur and is especially useful for fast-paced sports and gaming. However, when you watch TV shows or movies, it creates the infamous soap-opera effect. As a result, you get artificial and hyper-realistic visuals that kill the cinematic experience.
On my LG TV, I opened Settings -> Picture -> Advanced Settings -> Clarity -> TruMotion and turned it off. Once disabled, my TV produced more natural and immersive visuals when I’m watching my favorite shows. This is one of the best ways to get better performance on your TV.
Personalized content recommendations
Reduce personalization happening at TV operating-system level
Your smart TV can learn what you like, so it can show you more of it. Well, this might sound like the whole point of a smart TV. Now, this also means your TV is silently building a behavioral profile from everything you watch. Just like ACR, it can feed your data into the advertising pipeline. For instance, LG's current AI TV features such as AI Concierge are designed to tailor content suggestions to individual users.
I don't mind recommendations inside Netflix or another streaming service that I actively use. That's part of the reason I use those services. That said, I don’t want my TV to fill up my home screen with personalized recommendation rows. So, I went to Settings -> General -> System -> Additional Settings -> Home Settings and disabled Content Recommendation.
Voice recognition features
I was barely using them
Sure, voice control gives you convenience. Just say "turn on Netflix," and you can skip the remote entirely. However, I don’t even remember the last time I used voice control features. I have only used it a couple of times since I bought the TV, and the microphone kept listening in the background. My TV remote already has buttons for practically everything I need. I don't really need to talk to the TV to launch an app or change the volume for me.
My LG OLED TV also offers AI Voice ID that can recognize an individual's voice and build a personalized profile, showing recommendations and watchlists. It’s a useful feature for households where members have different profiles and actually want the TV to recognize who's speaking. I don’t need them, so I had no reason to keep voice recognition features on.
My TV feels better with less smart stuff
Turning these smart features off didn’t make my TV less capable. In fact, my TV now looks better and feels faster to navigate. It streams everything I want it to. The only difference is it doesn’t constantly try to sell something or personalize things I never asked for. If you have never explored your TV's settings menu beyond the picture mode, I would recommend spending a few minutes. You might be surprised how much better your TV can look and feel without unwanted smarter fluff.
LG evo AI C5 OLED TV
The LG evo AI C5 OLED TV is a solid buy for those looking for a relatively affordable but powerful and gorgeous looking OLED TV. With lots of built-in technologies to combat burn-in, it's not as big a problem as it was in the past.
articles.summary:
Smart TV owners can significantly improve their viewing experience and privacy by disabling intrusive features like home screen advertisements, motion smoothing, and background data tracking settings.

### Key Points
- Disable "Home Promotion" and "Autoplay" in system settings to remove cluttered advertisements and noisy video trailers from your home screen.
- Turn off Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to prevent the TV from tracking your viewing habits and sharing data with third-party advertisers.
- Deactivate default energy-saving modes to restore full brightness, contrast, and HDR performance for a more vibrant picture quality.
- Switch off motion smoothing features like TruMotion or Auto Motion Plus to eliminate the artificial "soap-opera effect" and preserve cinematic frame rates.
- Disable voice recognition and personalized content recommendations to reduce background data collection and minimize unwanted behavioral profiling.

### Why it Matters
Adjusting these settings allows users to reclaim control over their hardware, ensuring that high-end displays perform as intended without interference from intrusive marketing or tracking software. By optimizing these configurations, consumers can improve system responsiveness and protect their privacy while maintaining full access to their preferred streaming services.
